[[Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}} through the {{ill|Second Sino-Japanese War|ja|日中戦争}} and {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦}}. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩}} soldiers who died in the {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争}}. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == {{citation needed|Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja}} [[Category:Shinto shrines in Yamagata Prefecture]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Yamagata (city)]] [[Category:History of Yamagata (city)]] Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[Hatsumōde]] festival of [[Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. [[Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}} through the {{ill|Second Sino-Japanese War|ja|日中戦争}} and {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦}}. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩}} soldiers who died in the {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争}}. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == {{citation needed|Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja}} [[Category:Shinto shrines in Yamagata Prefecture]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Yamagata (city)]] [[Category:History of Yamagata (city)]] Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[Hatsumōde]] festival of [[Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. [[Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}} through the {{ill|Second Sino-Japanese War|ja|日中戦争}} and {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦}}. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩}} soldiers who died in the {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争}}. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == {{citation needed|Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja}} [[Category:Shinto shrines in Yamagata Prefecture]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Yamagata (city)]] [[Category:History of Yamagata (city)]] Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[Hatsumōde]] festival of [[Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. Second most is {{ill|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|simple|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|draft}} == See Also == * [[Controversies surrounding Yasukuni Shrine]] * [[Martyrs' shrines (China)|Martyr's [[Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}} through the {{ill|Second Sino-Japanese War|ja|日中戦争}} and {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦}}. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩}} soldiers who died in the {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争}}. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == {{citation needed|Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja}} [[Category:Shinto shrines in Yamagata Prefecture]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Yamagata (city)]] [[Category:History of Yamagata (city)]] Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[Hatsumōde]] festival of [[Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. Second most is {{ill|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|simple|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|draft}} == See Also == * [[Controversies surrounding Yasukuni Shrine]] * [[Martyrs' shrines (China)|Martyr's Shrines]] * [[:en:Martial temple|Martial temple]] and [[:en:Wen Wu temple|Wen Wu temple]] * [[National Revolutionary Martyrs' Shrine]] * [[Eternal Spring Shrine]] * [[:en:Chinese Cultural Renaissance|Chinese Cultural Renaissance]] * [[Ancestral shrine]] * [[:en:Gallant Garden|Gallant Garden]] * [[Gokoku Shrines]] * [[:en:Tomb of the Unknown Soldier|Tomb of the Unknown Soldier]] * [[:en:Arlington National Cemetery|Arlington National Cemetery]] * [[:en:Valhalla|Valhalla]] (home to the souls of fallen warriors in Scandinavian mythology) * [[:en:Walhalla (memorial)|Walhalla Shrine]] (a hall of fame in Germany honoring "commendable and honorable Germans") * [[Eternal Spring Shrine]] * [[The common end of myriad good deeds]] * [[:en:Greek hero cult|Greek hero cult]] == References == {{reflist}} == External Links == * [http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/ Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja Official Site] {{citation needed|Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja}} [[Category:Shinto shrines in Yamagata Prefecture]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Yamagata (city)]] [[Category:History of Yamagata (city)]] {{Draft categories| [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Gokoku shrines]] [[Category:Gokoku shrines]] {{Gokoku Shrines}} [[Category:Gokoku shrines]] [[Category:1869 establishments]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Yamagata Prefecture]] [[Category:Yamagata Prefecture]] [[category:drafts]] [[Category:Default sort converted to citation needed]] {{citation needed|Yamagata Gokoku Shrine}}[[Category:Ugoodbye $1 categories]] [[Category:deprecated qq open]]

Gokoku-jinja honden.jpg|220px]]
Haiden | caption = | map_type = Japan Yamagata | coordinates = {{coord|38|15|45.23|N|140|20|49.86|E|scale:25000_region:JP-06_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja}} | location = Yakushimachi 2-8-75, {{ill|Yamagata (city)|ja|山形市|lt=Yamagata City}}, {{ill|Yamagata Prefecture|ja|山形県}}, Japan | deity = Over 48,045 war dead spirits (Gokoku no eirei) | type = Former Ministry of Interior-designated Gokoku Jinja, {{ill|Beppyo Shrine|ja|別表神社}} | founded = {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治}} 2 ({{ill|1869|ja|1869年}}) | festival = {{ill|May 11|ja|5月11日}}, {{ill|November 2|ja|11月2日}} }} '''Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja''' (山形県護国神社) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} ({{ill|Gokoku Shrine|ja|護国神社}}) located in {{ill|Yamagata (city)|ja|山形市}}, {{ill|Yamagata Prefecture|ja|山形県}}. [[Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}} through the {{ill|Second Sino-Japanese War|ja|日中戦争}} and {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦}}. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩}} soldiers who died in the {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争}}. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == {{citation needed|Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja}} [[Category:Shinto shrines in Yamagata Prefecture]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Yamagata (city)]] [[Category:History of Yamagata (city)]] Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[Hatsumōde]] festival of [[Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. Second most is {{ill|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|simple|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|draft}} == See Also == * [[Controversies surrounding Yasukuni Shrine]] * [[Martyrs' shrines (China)|Martyr's [[Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}} through the {{ill|Second Sino-Japanese War|ja|日中戦争}} and {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦}}. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩}} soldiers who died in the {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争}}. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == {{citation needed|Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja}} [[Category:Shinto shrines in Yamagata Prefecture]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Yamagata (city)]] [[Category:History of Yamagata (city)]] Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[Hatsumōde]] festival of [[Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. Second most is {{ill|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|simple|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|draft}} == See Also == * [[Controversies surrounding Yasukuni Shrine]] * [[Martyrs' shrines (China)|Martyr's [[Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}} through the {{ill|Second Sino-Japanese War|ja|日中戦争}} and {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦}}. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩}} soldiers who died in the {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争}}. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == {{citation needed|Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja}} [[Category:Shinto shrines in Yamagata Prefecture]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Yamagata (city)]] [[Category:History of Yamagata (city)]] Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[Hatsumōde]] festival of [[Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. Second most is {{ill|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|simple|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|draft}} == See Also == * [[Controversies surrounding Yasukuni Shrine]] * [[Martyrs' shrines (China)|Martyr's [[Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}} through the {{ill|Second Sino-Japanese War|ja|日中戦争}} and {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦}}. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩}} soldiers who died in the {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争}}. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == {{citation needed|Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja}} [[Category:Shinto shrines in Yamagata Prefecture]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Yamagata (city)]] [[Category:History of Yamagata (city)]] Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[Hatsumōde]] festival of [[Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. Haiden | caption = | map_type = Japan Yamagata | coordinates = {{coord|38|15|45.23|N|140|20|49.86|E|scale:25000_region:JP-06_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja}} | location = Yakushimachi 2-8-75, {{ill|Yamagata (city)|ja|山形市|lt=Yamagata City}}, {{ill|Yamagata Prefecture|ja|山形県}}, Japan | deity = Over 48,045 war dead spirits (Gokoku no eirei) | type = Former Ministry of Interior-designated Gokoku Jinja, {{ill|Beppyo Shrine|ja|別表神社}} | founded = {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治}} 2 ({{ill|1869|ja|1869年}}) | festival = {{ill|May 11|ja|5月11日}}, {{ill|November 2|ja|11月2日}} }} '''Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja''' (山形県護国神社) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} ({{ill|Gokoku Shrine|ja|護国神社}}) located in {{ill|Yamagata (city)|ja|山形市}}, {{ill|Yamagata Prefecture|ja|山形県}}. [[Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}} through the {{ill|Second Sino-Japanese War|ja|日中戦争}} and {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦}}. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩}} soldiers who died in the {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争}}. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == {{citation needed|Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja}} [[Category:Shinto shrines in Yamagata Prefecture]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Yamagata (city)]] [[Category:History of Yamagata (city)]] Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[Hatsumōde]] festival of [[Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. Second most is {{ill|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|simple|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|draft}} == See Also == * [[Controversies surrounding Yasukuni Shrine]] * [[Martyrs' shrines (China)|Martyr's It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}} through the {{ill|Second Sino-Japanese War|ja|日中戦争}} and {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦}}. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩}} soldiers who died in the {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争}}. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[Hatsumōde]] festival of [[Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. [[Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}} through the {{ill|Second Sino-Japanese War|ja|日中戦争}} and {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦}}. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩}} soldiers who died in the {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争}}. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == {{citation needed|Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja}} [[Category:Shinto shrines in Yamagata Prefecture]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Yamagata (city)]] [[Category:History of Yamagata (city)]] Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[Hatsumōde]] festival of [[Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. Second most is {{ill|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|simple|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|draft}} == See Also == * [[Controversies surrounding Yasukuni Shrine]] * [[Martyrs' shrines (China)|Martyr's [[Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}} through the {{ill|Second Sino-Japanese War|ja|日中戦争}} and {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦}}. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩}} soldiers who died in the {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争}}. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == {{citation needed|Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja}} [[Category:Shinto shrines in Yamagata Prefecture]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Yamagata (city)]] [[Category:History of Yamagata (city)]] Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[Hatsumōde]] festival of [[Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. [[Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}} through the {{ill|Second Sino-Japanese War|ja|日中戦争}} and {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦}}. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩}} soldiers who died in the {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争}}. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == {{citation needed|Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja}} [[Category:Shinto shrines in Yamagata Prefecture]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Yamagata (city)]] [[Category:History of Yamagata (city)]] Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[Hatsumōde]] festival of [[Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. Second most is {{ill|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|simple|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|draft}}== See Also == * [[Controversies surrounding Yasukuni Shrine]] * [[Martyrs' shrines (China)|Martyr's [[Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}} through the {{ill|Second Sino-Japanese War|ja|日中戦争}} and {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦}}. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩}} soldiers who died in the {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争}}. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == {{citation needed|Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja}} [[Category:Shinto shrines in Yamagata Prefecture]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Yamagata (city)]] [[Category:History of Yamagata (city)]] Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[Hatsumōde]] festival of [[Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. Second most is {{ill|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|simple|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|draft}} == See Also == * [[Controversies surrounding Yasukuni Shrine]] * [[Martyrs' shrines (China)|Martyr's Renaissance|Chinese Cultural Renaissance]] * [[Ancestral shrine]] * [[:en:Gallant Garden|Gallant Garden]] * [[Gokoku Shrines]] * [[:en:Tomb of the Unknown Soldier|Tomb of the Unknown Soldier]] * It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新|12=draft}} through the {{ill|Second Sino-Japanese War|ja|日中戦争|12=draft}} and {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦|12=draft}}. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩|12=draft}} soldiers who died in the {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争|12=draft}}. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|12=draft}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == {{citation needed|Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja}} Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|12=draft}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[Hatsumōde]] festival of [[Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. Second most is {{ill|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|simple|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|draft|12=draft}} == See Also == * [[Controversies surrounding Yasukuni Shrine]] * [[Martyrs' shrines [[Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新|12=draft}} through the {{ill|Second Sino-Japanese War|ja|日中戦争|12=draft}} and {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦|12=draft}}. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩|12=draft}} soldiers who died in the {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争|12=draft}}. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|12=draft}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == {{citation needed|Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja}} Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|12=draft}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[Hatsumōde]] festival of [[Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. Second most is {{ill|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|simple|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|draft|12=draft}} == See Also == * [[Controversies surrounding Yasukuni Shrine]] * [[Martyrs' shrines [[Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新|12=draft|12=draft}} through the {{ill|Second Sino-Japanese War|ja|日中戦争|12=draft|12=draft}} and {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦|12=draft|12=draft}}. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩|12=draft|12=draft}} soldiers who died in the {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争|12=draft|12=draft}}. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|12=draft|12=draft}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == {{citation needed|Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja}} Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|12=draft|12=draft}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[Hatsumōde]] festival of [[Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. Second most is {{ill|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|simple|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|draft|12=draft|12=draft}} == See Also == * [[Controversies surrounding Yasukuni Shrine]] * [[Martyrs' shrines In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == {{citation needed|Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja}} Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[Hatsumōde]] festival of [[Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. [[Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新|12=draft|12=draft}} through the {{ill|Second Sino-Japanese War|ja|日中戦争|12=draft|12=draft}} and {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦|12=draft|12=draft}}. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩|12=draft|12=draft}} soldiers who died in the {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争|12=draft|12=draft}}. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|12=draft|12=draft}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == {{citation needed|Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja}} Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|12=draft|12=draft}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[Hatsumōde]] festival of [[Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. [[Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新|qq=draft|qq=draft}} through the {{ill|Second Sino-Japanese War|ja|日中戦争|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩|qq=draft|qq=draft}} soldiers who died in the {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == {{citation needed|Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja}} Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[Hatsumōde]] festival of [[Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. Second most is {{ill|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|simple|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|draft|qq=draft|qq=draft}} == See Also == * [[Controversies surrounding Yasukuni Shrine]] * [[Martyrs' shrines [[Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新|qq=draft|qq=draft}} through the {{ill|Second Sino-Japanese War|ja|日中戦争|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩|qq=draft|qq=draft}} soldiers who died in the {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == {{citation needed|Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja}} Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[Hatsumōde]] festival of [[Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. Second most is {{ill|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|simple|Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|draft|qq=draft|qq=draft}} == See Also == * [[Controversies surrounding Yasukuni Shrine]] * [[Martyrs' shrines (China)|Martyr's Shrines]] * [[:en:Martial temple|Martial temple]] and [[:en:Wen Wu temple|Wen Wu temple]] * [[National Revolutionary Martyrs' Shrine]] * [[Eternal Spring Shrine]] * [[:en:Chinese Cultural Renaissance|Chinese Cultural Renaissance]] * [[Ancestral shrine]] * [[:en:Gallant Garden|Gallant Garden]] * [[Gokoku Shrines]] * [[:en:Tomb of the Unknown Soldier|Tomb of the Unknown Soldier]] * [[:en:Arlington National Cemetery|Arlington National Cemetery]] * [[:en:Valhalla|Valhalla]] (home to the souls of fallen warriors in Scandinavian mythology) * [[:en:Walhalla (memorial)|Walhalla Shrine]] (a hall of fame in Germany honoring "commendable and honorable Germans") * [[Eternal Spring Shrine]] * [[The common end of myriad good deeds]] * [[:en:Greek hero cult|Greek hero cult]] == References == {{reflist}} == External Links == * [http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/ Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja Official Site] {{citation needed|Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja}} {{citation needed|Yamagata Gokoku Shrine}}{{citation needed|Yamagata Gokoku Shrine}}{{citation needed|Yamagata Gokoku Shrine}}{{citation needed|Yamagata Gokoku Shrine}} }}{{Shinto-stub}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ \ }} {{citation needed|Yamagata Gokoku Shrine}} {{translated page|ja|山形県護国神社|version=91319277|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{Draft categories| {{Gokoku Shrines}} [[simple:user:immanuelle/Yamagata Gokoku Shrine]] [[sn:Yamagata Gokoku Shrine]] [[ja:山形県護国神社]] [[en:Yamagata Gokoku Shrine]] [[sn:amagata Gokoku Shrine]]
