[[Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo Shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji Restoration|qq=}} through the {{ill|Second Sino-Japanese War|ja|日中戦争|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Second Sino-Japanese War|qq=}} and {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/World War II|qq=}}. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Satsuma Domain|qq=}} soldiers who died in the {{ill|Boshin War|ja|戊辰戦争|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Boshin War|qq=}}. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōkonsha|qq=}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|qq=}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[Hatsumōde]] festival of [[Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. Second most is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|simple|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|qq=}} == See Also == * [[Controversies surrounding Yasukuni Shrine]] * [[Martyrs' shrines (China)|Martyr's Shrines]] * [[:en:Martial temple|Martial temple]] and [[:en:Wen Wu temple|Wen Wu temple]] * [[National Revolutionary Martyrs' Shrine]] * [[Eternal Spring Shrine]] * [[:en:Chinese Cultural Renaissance|Chinese Cultural Renaissance]] * [[Ancestral shrine]] * [[:en:Gallant Garden|Gallant Garden]] * [[Gokoku Shrines]] * [[:en:Tomb of the Unknown Soldier|Tomb of the Unknown Soldier]] * [[:en:Arlington National Cemetery|Arlington National Cemetery]] * [[:en:Valhalla|Valhalla]] (home to the souls of fallen warriors in Scandinavian mythology) * [[:en:Walhalla (memorial)|Walhalla Shrine]] (a hall of fame in Germany honoring "commendable and honorable Germans") * [[Eternal Spring Shrine]] * [[The common end of myriad good deeds]] * [[:en:Greek hero cult|Greek hero cult]] == References == {{reflist}} == External Links == * [http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/ Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja Official Site] }}{{Shinto-stub}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ \ }} {{translated page|ja|山形県護国神社|version=91319277|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{Draft categories| {{Gokoku Shrines}} [[simple:user:immanuelle/Yamagata Gokoku Shrine]] [[sn:Yamagata Gokoku Shrine]] [[ja:山形県護国神社]] [[en:Yamagata Gokoku Shrine]] [[sn:amagata Gokoku Shrine]]

Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten [[:en:Satsuma Domain|Satsuma Domain]] soldiers who died in the [[:en:Boshin War|Boshin War]]. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten [[:en:Satsuma Domain|Satsuma Domain]] soldiers who died in the [[:en:Boshin War|Boshin War]]. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten [[:en:Satsuma Domain|Satsuma Domain]] soldiers who died in the [[:en:Boshin War|Boshin War]]. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten [[:en:Satsuma Domain|Satsuma Domain]] soldiers who died in the [[:en:Boshin War|Boshin War]]. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo Shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[:en:Yamagata Prefecture|Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[:en:Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the [[:en:Meiji Restoration|Meiji Restoration]] through the [[:en:Second Sino-Japanese War|Second Sino-Japanese War]] and [[:en:World War II|World War II]]. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten [[:en:Satsuma Domain|Satsuma Domain]] soldiers who died in the [[:en:Boshin War|Boshin War]]. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōkonsha|qq=|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Shokonsha|WD=Q11497810}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|qq=}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[:en:Hatsumōde|Hatsumōde]] festival of [[:en:Yamagata Prefecture|Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. Second most is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|simple|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|qq=}} == See Also == * [[Controversies surrounding Yasukuni Shrine]] * [[:en:Martyrs' shrines (China)|Martyr's Shrines]] * [[:en:Martial temple|Martial temple]] and [[:en:Wen Wu temple|Wen Wu temple]] * [[:en:National Revolutionary Martyrs' Shrine|National Revolutionary Martyrs' Shrine]] * [[:en:Eternal Spring Shrine|Eternal Spring Shrine]] * [[:en:Chinese Cultural Renaissance|Chinese Cultural Renaissance]] * [[Ancestral shrine]] * [[:en:Gallant Garden|Gallant Garden]] * [[Gokoku Shrines]] * [[:en:Tomb of the Unknown Soldier|Tomb of the Unknown Soldier]] * [[:en:Arlington National Cemetery|Arlington National Cemetery]] * [[:en:Valhalla|Valhalla]] (home to the souls of fallen warriors in Scandinavian mythology) * [[:en:Walhalla (memorial)|Walhalla Shrine]] (a hall of fame in Germany honoring "commendable and honorable Germans") * [[:en:Eternal Spring Shrine|Eternal Spring Shrine]] * [[:en:The common end of myriad good deeds|The common end of myriad good deeds]] * [[:en:Greek hero cult|Greek hero cult]] == References == {{reflist}} == External Links == * [http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/ Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja Official Site] }}{{Shinto-stub}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ \ }} {{translated page|ja|山形県護国神社|version=91319277|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{Draft categories| {{Gokoku Shrines}} [[sn:User:Immanuelle/Yamagata Gokoku Shrine]] [[sn:Yamagata Gokoku Shrine]] [[ja:山形県護国神社]] [[sn:amagata Gokoku Shrine]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Buildings in Yamagata, Yamagata]] [[Category:History of Yamagata, Yamagata]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Yamagata Prefecture]] [[Category:Gokoku shrines]] [[Category:pages with former wikipedia userpage links]] {{Commons category|Yamagataken-Gokoku-jinja}}

[[:en:Japan|Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo Shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[:en:Yamagata Prefecture|Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[:en:Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten [[:en:Satsuma Domain|Satsuma Domain]] soldiers who died in the [[:en:Boshin War|Boshin War]]. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōkonsha|qq=|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Shokonsha|WD=Q11497810}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|qq=}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[:en:Hatsumōde|Hatsumōde]] festival of [[:en:Yamagata Prefecture|Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. (Formerly ''[[Shokonsha]]'') | leadership = | website = | architecture_style = | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = |Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| name = Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja (Yamagata Prefectural Gokoku Shrine) | caption = | map_type = Japan Yamagata | location = Yakushimachi 2-8-75, [[:en:Yamagata (city)|Yamagata City]], [[:en:Yamagata Prefecture|Yamagata Prefecture]], Japan | deity = Over 48,045 war dead spirits (Gokoku no eirei) | type = Former Ministry of Interior-designated Gokoku Jinja, [[:en:Beppyo shrine|Beppyo Shrine]] | founded = [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]] 2 ([[:en:1869|1869]]) | festival = [[:en:May 11|May 11]], [[:en:November 2|November 2]] | prefecture= {{ill|Yamagata|WD=Q205526}} }} '''Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja''' (山形県護国神社) is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] ([[:en:Gokoku shrines|Gokoku Shrine]]) located in [[:en:Yamagata (city)|Yamagata (city)]], [[:en:Yamagata Prefecture|Yamagata Prefecture]]. [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo Shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[:en:Yamagata Prefecture|Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[:en:Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the [[:en:Meiji Restoration|Meiji Restoration]] through the [[:en:Second Sino-Japanese War|Second Sino-Japanese War]] and [[:en:World War II|World War II]]. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten [[:en:Satsuma Domain|Satsuma Domain]] soldiers who died in the [[:en:Boshin War|Boshin War]]. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōkonsha|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Shokonsha|WD=Q11497810}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|qq=}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[:en:Hatsumōde|Hatsumōde]] festival of [[:en:Yamagata Prefecture|Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. Second most is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|simple|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|qq=}} == See Also == * [[Controversies surrounding Yasukuni (Formerly ''[[Shokonsha]]'') | leadership = | website = | architecture_style = | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = |Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| name = Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja (Yamagata Prefectural Gokoku Shrine) | caption = | map_type = Japan Yamagata | location = Yakushimachi 2-8-75, [[:en:Yamagata (city)|Yamagata City]], [[:en:Yamagata Prefecture|Yamagata Prefecture]], Japan | deity = Over 48,045 war dead spirits (Gokoku no eirei) | type = Former Ministry of Interior-designated Gokoku Jinja, [[:en:Beppyo shrine|Beppyo Shrine]] | founded = [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]] 2 ([[:en:1869|1869]]) | festival = [[:en:May 11|May 11]], [[:en:November 2|November 2]] | prefecture= {{ill|Yamagata|WD=Q205526}} }} '''Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja''' (山形県護国神社) is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] ([[:en:Gokoku shrines|Gokoku Shrine]]) located in [[:en:Yamagata (city)|Yamagata (city)]], [[:en:Yamagata Prefecture|Yamagata Prefecture]]. [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo Shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[:en:Yamagata Prefecture|Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[:en:Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the [[:en:Meiji Restoration|Meiji Restoration]] through the [[:en:Second Sino-Japanese War|Second Sino-Japanese War]] and [[:en:World War II|World War II]]. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten [[:en:Satsuma Domain|Satsuma Domain]] soldiers who died in the [[:en:Boshin War|Boshin War]]. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōkonsha|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Shokonsha|WD=Q11497810}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|qq=}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[:en:Hatsumōde|Hatsumōde]] festival of [[:en:Yamagata Prefecture|Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. Second most is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|simple|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|qq=}} == See Also == * [[Controversies surrounding Yasukuni It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[:en:Yamagata Prefecture|Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[:en:Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the [[:en:Meiji Restoration|Meiji Restoration]] through the [[:en:Second Sino-Japanese War|Second Sino-Japanese War]] and [[:en:World War II|World War II]]. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten [[:en:Satsuma Domain|Satsuma Domain]] soldiers who died in the [[:en:Boshin War|Boshin War]]. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōkonsha|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Shokonsha|WD=Q11497810}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|qq=}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[:en:Hatsumōde|Hatsumōde]] festival of [[:en:Yamagata Prefecture|Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. Second most is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|simple|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|qq=}} == See Also == * [[Controversies surrounding Yasukuni Shrine]] * [[:en:Martyrs' shrines (China)|Martyr's Shrines]] * [[:en:Martial temple|Martial temple]] and [[:en:Wen Wu temple|Wen Wu temple]] * [[:en:National Revolutionary Martyrs' Shrine|National Revolutionary Martyrs' Shrine]] * [[:en:Eternal Spring Shrine|Eternal Spring Shrine]] * [[:en:Chinese Cultural Renaissance|Chinese Cultural Renaissance]] * [[Ancestral shrine]] * [[:en:Gallant Garden|Gallant Garden]] * [[Gokoku Shrines]] * [[:en:Tomb of the Unknown Soldier|Tomb of the Unknown Soldier]] * [[:en:Arlington National Cemetery|Arlington National Cemetery]] * [[:en:Valhalla|Valhalla]] (home to the souls of fallen warriors in Scandinavian mythology) * [[:en:Walhalla (memorial)|Walhalla Shrine]] (a hall of fame in Germany honoring "commendable and honorable Germans") * [[:en:Eternal Spring Shrine|Eternal Spring Shrine]] * [[:en:The common end of myriad good deeds|The common end of myriad good deeds]] * [[:en:Greek hero cult|Greek hero cult]] == References == {{reflist}} == External Links == * [http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/ Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja Official Site] }}{{Shinto-stub}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ \ }} {{translated page|ja|山形県護国神社|version=91319277|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{Draft categories| {{Gokoku Shrines}} [[ja:山形県護国神社]] {{Commons category|Yamagataken-Gokoku-jinja}} {{wikidata link|Q11468583}} [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Buildings in Yamagata, Yamagata]] [[Category:Gokoku shrines]] [[Category:History of Yamagata, Yamagata]] [[Category:pages with conflicting qids]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Yamagata Prefecture]] [[Category:Wikidata has English label]] [[Category:Wikidata has short description]]

[[:en:Japan|Japan]]. It is a [[Beppyo Shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in [[:en:Yamagata Prefecture|Yamagata Prefecture]].{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[:en:Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the [[:en:Meiji Restoration|Meiji Restoration]] through the [[:en:Second Sino-Japanese War|Second Sino-Japanese War]] and [[:en:World War II|World War II]]. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten [[:en:Satsuma Domain|Satsuma Domain]] soldiers who died in the [[:en:Boshin War|Boshin War]]. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōkonsha|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Shokonsha|WD=Q11497810}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|qq=}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest [[:en:Hatsumōde|Hatsumōde]] festival of [[:en:Yamagata Prefecture|Yamagata Prefecture]] with 130,000 people attending. Second most is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|simple|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|qq=}} == See Also == * [[Controversies surrounding Yasukuni Shrine]] * [[:en:Martyrs' shrines (China)|Martyr's Shrines]] * [[:en:Martial temple|Martial temple]] and [[:en:Wen Wu temple|Wen Wu temple]] * [[:en:National Revolutionary Martyrs' Shrine|National Revolutionary Martyrs' Shrine]] * [[:en:Eternal Spring Shrine|Eternal Spring Shrine]] * [[:en:Chinese Cultural Renaissance|Chinese Cultural Renaissance]] * [[Ancestral shrine]] * [[:en:Gallant Garden|Gallant Garden]] * [[Gokoku Shrines]] * [[:en:Tomb of the Unknown Soldier|Tomb of the Unknown Soldier]] * [[:en:Arlington National Cemetery|Arlington National Cemetery]] * [[:en:Valhalla|Valhalla]] (home to the souls of fallen warriors in Scandinavian mythology) * [[:en:Walhalla (memorial)|Walhalla Shrine]] (a hall of fame in Germany honoring "commendable and honorable Germans") * [[:en:Eternal Spring Shrine|Eternal Spring Shrine]] * [[:en:The common end of myriad good deeds|The common end of myriad good deeds]] * [[:en:Greek hero cult|Greek hero cult]] == References == {{reflist}} == External Links == * [http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/ Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja Official Site] }}{{Shinto-stub}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ \ }} {{translated page|ja|山形県護国神社|version=91319277|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{Draft categories| {{Gokoku Shrines}} [[ja:山形県護国神社]] {{Commons category|Yamagataken-Gokoku-jinja}} {{wikidata link|Q11468583}} [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Buildings in Yamagata, Yamagata]] [[Category:Gokoku shrines]] [[Category:History of Yamagata, Yamagata]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Yamagata Prefecture]] [[Category:Wikidata has English label]] [[Category:Wikidata has short description]]

In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Gokoku-jinja honden.jpg | map_type = Japan | coordinates ={{Coord|38.26255555555556|N|140.34719444444445|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | map_size = | map_alt = | map_relief = | map_caption = | location = | festival = | type = ''[[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]]''
(Formerly ''[[Shokonsha]]'') | leadership = | website = | architecture_style = | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = |Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| name = Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja (Yamagata Prefectural Gokoku Shrine) | caption = | map_type = Japan Yamagata | location = Yakushimachi 2-8-75, {{ill|Yamagata (city)|en|Yamagata (city)|WD=Q205526|lt=Yamagata City}}, {{ill|Yamagata Prefecture|en|Yamagata Prefecture|WD=Q125863|lt=Yamagata Prefecture}}, Japan | deity = Over 48,045 war dead spirits (Gokoku no eirei) | type = Former Ministry of Interior-designated Gokoku Jinja, {{ill|Beppyo shrine|en|Beppyo shrine|WD=Q10898274|lt=Beppyo Shrine}} | founded = {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era}} 2 ({{ill|1869|en|1869|WD=Q7720|lt=1869}}) | festival = {{ill|May 11|en|May 11|WD=Q2558|lt=May 11}}, {{ill|November 2|en|November 2|WD=Q2996|lt=November 2}} | prefecture= {{ill|Yamagata|WD=Q205526}} }} '''Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja''' (山形県護国神社) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} ({{ill|Gokoku shrines|en|Gokoku shrines|WD=Q1534477|lt=Gokoku Shrine}}) located in {{ill|Yamagata (city)|en|Yamagata (city)|WD=Q205526|lt=Yamagata (city)}}, {{ill|Yamagata Prefecture|en|Yamagata Prefecture|WD=Q125863|lt=Yamagata Prefecture}}. {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan}}. It is a [[Beppyo Shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in {{ill|Yamagata Prefecture|en|Yamagata Prefecture|WD=Q125863|lt=Yamagata Prefecture}}.{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of {{ill|Yasukuni Shrine|en|Yasukuni Shrine|WD=Q242803|lt=Yasukuni Shrine}}. They were renamed from {{ill|Shōkonsha|en|Shōkonsha|WD=Q11497810|lt=Shokonsha}} in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|en|Meiji Restoration|WD=Q8707|lt=Meiji Restoration}} through the {{ill|Second Sino-Japanese War|en|Second Sino-Japanese War|WD=Q170314|lt=Second Sino-Japanese War}} and {{ill|World War II|en|World War II|WD=Q362|lt=World War II}}. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten {{ill|Satsuma Domain|en|Satsuma Domain|WD=Q676187|lt=Satsuma Domain}} soldiers who died in the {{ill|Boshin War|en|Boshin War|WD=Q309184|lt=Boshin War}}. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōkonsha|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Shokonsha|WD=Q11497810}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|qq=}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest {{ill|Hatsumōde|en|Hatsumōde|WD=Q1032381|lt=Hatsumōde}} festival of {{ill|Yamagata Prefecture|en|Yamagata Prefecture|WD=Q125863|lt=Yamagata Prefecture}} with 130,000 people attending. Second most is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|simple|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu|qq=}} == See Also == * [[Controversies surrounding Yasukuni It was founded in 1868, and is located in {{ill|Yamagata Prefecture|en|Yamagata Prefecture|WD=Q125863|lt=Yamagata Prefecture|1=Yamagata Prefecture}}.{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. They were renamed from {{ill|Shōkonsha|en|Shōkonsha|WD=Q11497810|lt=Shokonsha|1=Shōkonsha}} in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten {{ill|Satsuma Domain|en|Satsuma Domain|WD=Q676187|lt=Satsuma Domain|1=Satsuma Domain}} soldiers who died in the {{ill|Boshin War|en|Boshin War|WD=Q309184|lt=Boshin War|1=Boshin War}}. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōkonsha|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Shōkonsha|WD=Q11497810}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|qq=}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest {{ill|Hatsumōde|en|Hatsumōde|WD=Q1032381|lt=Hatsumōde|1=Hatsumōde}} festival of {{ill|Yamagata Prefecture|en|Yamagata Prefecture|WD=Q125863|lt=Yamagata Prefecture|1=Yamagata Prefecture}} with 130,000 people attending. (Formerly ''[[Shokonsha]]'') | leadership = | website = | architecture_style = | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = |Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| name = Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja (Yamagata Prefectural Gokoku Shrine) | caption = | map_type = Japan Yamagata | location = Yakushimachi 2-8-75, {{ill|Yamagata (city)|en|Yamagata (city)|WD=Q205526|lt=Yamagata City|1=Yamagata (city)}}, {{ill|Yamagata Prefecture|en|Yamagata Prefecture|WD=Q125863|lt=Yamagata Prefecture|1=Yamagata Prefecture}}, Japan | deity = Over 48,045 war dead spirits (Gokoku no eirei) | type = Former Ministry of Interior-designated Gokoku Jinja, {{ill|Beppyo shrine|en|Beppyo shrine|WD=Q10898274|lt=Beppyo Shrine|1=Beppyo shrine}} | founded = {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era|1=Meiji era}} 2 ({{ill|1869|en|1869|WD=Q7720|lt=1869|1=1869}}) | festival = {{ill|May 11|en|May 11|WD=Q2558|lt=May 11|1=May 11}}, {{ill|November 2|en|November 2|WD=Q2996|lt=November 2|1=November 2}} | prefecture= {{ill|Yamagata|WD=Q205526|1=Yamagata (city)}} }} '''Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja''' (山形県護国神社) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} ({{ill|Gokoku shrines|en|Gokoku shrines|WD=Q1534477|lt=Gokoku Shrine|1=Gokoku Shrines}}) located in {{ill|Yamagata (city)|en|Yamagata (city)|WD=Q205526|lt=Yamagata (city)|1=Yamagata (city)}}, {{ill|Yamagata Prefecture|en|Yamagata Prefecture|WD=Q125863|lt=Yamagata Prefecture|1=Yamagata Prefecture}}. {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}. It is a [[Beppyo Shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it. It was founded in 1868, and is located in {{ill|Yamagata Prefecture|en|Yamagata Prefecture|WD=Q125863|lt=Yamagata Prefecture|1=Yamagata Prefecture}}.{{Cite web |last=Yassan |date=2021-11-29 |title=Tiger in Yamagata prefecture Gokoku shrine, Yamagata City 25km |url=https://gpsart.info/en/tohoku-2/tiger-in-yamagata-prefecture-gokoku-shrine-yamagata-city-25km/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=GPS Art .info |language=en-GB}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead. Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of {{ill|Yasukuni Shrine|en|Yasukuni Shrine|WD=Q242803|lt=Yasukuni Shrine|1=Yasukuni Shrine}}. They were renamed from {{ill|Shōkonsha|en|Shōkonsha|WD=Q11497810|lt=Shokonsha|1=Shōkonsha}} in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |doi=10.1093/jcs/32.3.527 |jstor=23917081 |issn=0021-969X}} It enshrines over 48,000 spirits of those from Yamagata Prefecture who died in wars from the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|en|Meiji Restoration|WD=Q8707|lt=Meiji Restoration|1=Meiji Restoration}} through the {{ill|Second Sino-Japanese War|en|Second Sino-Japanese War|WD=Q170314|lt=Second Sino-Japanese War|1=Second Sino-Japanese War}} and {{ill|World War II|en|World War II|WD=Q362|lt=World War II|1=World War II}}. [[File:Yamagata Pref. Gokoku-jinja longshot.jpg|thumb|250px|Ōtorii (and haiden in the background)]] == History == The shrine traces its origins to Meiji 2 (1869), when a hall was constructed in Yōka-chō, Yamagata City, to enshrine the spirits of ten {{ill|Satsuma Domain|en|Satsuma Domain|WD=Q676187|lt=Satsuma Domain|1=Satsuma Domain}} soldiers who died in the {{ill|Boshin War|en|Boshin War|WD=Q309184|lt=Boshin War|1=Boshin War}}. In Meiji 8, it was designated as Yamagata {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōkonsha|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Shōkonsha|WD=Q11497810}}, and subsequently enshrined war dead from Yamagata Prefecture. In Meiji 22 (1889), it was relocated to Miyamachi, Yamagata City, but was destroyed by fire in a large blaze in 1911 (Meiji 44), and rebuilt in 1914 (Taishō 3). In Shōwa 9 (1934), it moved to its current location inside Chitose Park. In Shōwa 14 (1939), with institutional reforms, it was designated as an Interior Minister-approved Gokoku Jinja and named Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja. Under the Allied Occupation, from Shōwa 22 (1947) to Shōwa 27 (1952), it was called “Chitose-gū,” referencing Chitose Park. The current haiden was rebuilt in Heisei 6 (1994). == Hatsumōde (First Shrine Visit of the New Year) == Yamagata-ken Gokoku Jinja attracts the largest number of hatsumōde (New Year’s first visits) worshippers in Yamagata Prefecture, with about 130,000 visitors annually.[http://www.yamagataken-gokokujinja.jp/history.shtml Official site: History (in Japanese)][http://yamagata-np.jp/news/200901/05/kj_2009010500051.php “91,6000 People Visit Shrines in the Prefecture for New Year: Up by 33,000 from Last Year”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 5, 2009), accessed September 7, 2011.[http://yamagata-np.jp/news/201101/04/kj_2011010400048.php “Over 1 Million Visit Shrines for Hatsumōde in Prefecture, Highest in a Decade”] Yamagata Shimbun (January 4, 2011), accessed September 7, 2011. The second most visited shrine is {{ill|Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|ja|鳥海月山両所宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gū|qq=}} in Yamagata City (~110,000 visitors). Only these two shrines surpass 100,000 visitors in the prefecture. == New years festival == The shrine has the largest {{ill|Hatsumōde|en|Hatsumōde|WD=Q1032381|lt=Hatsumōde|1=Hatsumōde}} festival of {{ill|Yamagata Prefecture|en|Yamagata Prefecture|WD=Q125863|lt=Yamagata Prefecture|1=Yamagata Prefecture}} with 130,000 people attending.
